docs.title: SigGear | Custom Precision Transmission Manufacturing
docs.text:
SigGear develops and manufactures custom compact transmission solutions for engineering teams that need more than a catalog product.

The standard products published on this site are public reference platforms. They show real transmission architectures, manufacturing scope, technical data and design-in resources that can be shared openly. They represent only the part of SigGear's work that can be published.

A significant part of SigGear's engineering and manufacturing work is customer-specific and cannot be shown publicly because the products, drawings, mechanisms and project details are protected by confidentiality agreements.

SigGear's core capability is therefore broader than the public catalog:

  • custom planetary gearboxes and compact reducers
  • custom cycloidal transmissions and robot joint modules
  • motor + gearbox integration around a customer-selected motor
  • custom ratios, shafts, flanges, housings and mechanical interfaces
  • prototype development, testing and design refinement
  • repeatable volume manufacturing after configuration freeze
  • production planning and delivery for volume programs
  • machining, gear processing, assembly, inspection and validation in a real manufacturing environment

docs.title: Start a Custom Transmission Engineering Review
docs.text:
You do not need to know a SigGear model number before contacting us.

The published products, datasheets and STEP files are public reference platforms, not the boundary of SigGear's custom manufacturing capability.

Most custom projects can start from one of four situations:

  • “Here is my motor.” — the motor is already selected and the transmission must fit it.
  • “Here is our drawing / STEP / sample.” — the mechanism, STEP model, physical sample or installation envelope defines the starting interface.
  • “Our existing gearbox needs replacement / redesign.” — the motor or machine interface may need to stay while ratio, output, durability or other gearbox details change.
  • “We need prototypes first, then volume production.” — the project needs a path from sample validation into repeatable manufacturing.

If you already know a SigGear model, include it as a reference. If not, send the application and the information you already have. A complete specification is not required for the first review.

If the project specifically needs a micro, miniature or compact planetary gearbox, see Custom Planetary Gearbox Engineering.

If the project involves a compact high-torque joint or a possible cycloidal structure, see Custom Cycloidal Transmission Engineering.

If the project starts from an existing motor or needs a complete motor + gearbox solution, see Motor + Gearbox Integration Engineering.

If the project is a robot joint, compact actuator or AI-hardware rotary axis with custom torque, speed, size, sensing or control requirements, see Custom Robot Joint & Compact Actuator Development.

If the project has moved beyond a first concept and needs a structured path through prototype, testing, Design-In, pilot preparation and production release, see Prototype to Design-In and Production.

Path A: Planetary Gearbox for an Existing Motor
docs.text:
Choose this path when the motor is already selected and you need SigGear to review a compatible planetary gearbox.

For the first review, send only what you already know:

  1. Motor model or drawing
  2. Motor speed
  3. Motor shaft diameter / usable shaft length
  4. Motor mounting pattern / locating pilot
  5. Required output speed or ratio
  6. Maximum gearbox / assembly diameter and length
  7. Load or torque, if known

If torque or an interface dimension is not known, a motor drawing or mechanism sketch is enough to start.

docs.title: Minimum Information to Start
docs.text:
For a first engineering review, you can start with the problem rather than a complete product specification.

Four items are usually enough:

  1. Application — what is moving and where the gearbox / actuator will be installed
  2. Required output — torque and speed if known
  3. Installation limit — maximum diameter, length or a simple sketch if available
  4. What you need next — model recommendation, STEP / drawing review, sample, replacement review or quotation

If you do not know the reduction ratio, send the motor speed and desired output speed if available.

docs.title: Helpful Information When Available
docs.text:
The following helps narrow the configuration but does not need to be sent all at once:

  • company name and country
  • project stage: concept, prototype, pilot or production
  • continuous and peak torque
  • peak duration
  • operating voltage
  • motor information for gearbox-only projects
  • output shaft / mounting requirement
  • duty cycle and peak duration
  • failure symptoms / worn-part evidence for replacement projects
  • radial / axial load conditions
  • driver, encoder and communication requirements
  • prototype quantity and estimated annual volume
  • target schedule
  • whether NDA / confidentiality is required
  • delivery destination

A mechanism sketch with key dimensions is acceptable for the first review.

docs.title: What You Can Request
docs.text:

  • mechanical-interface review
  • prototype sample evaluation
  • motor + gearbox matching
  • driver / encoder / communication review for applicable products
  • quotation preparation

Technical files and final configuration details depend on the selected model and engineering review.

docs.title: What Does a Dexterous-Hand Engineer Need to Define?
docs.text:
A useful first selection usually needs:

  • Mechanism type — tendon spool, direct rotary finger joint, linkage, screw or jaw mechanism
  • Required force / load — fingertip force, tendon pull or mechanism resistance
  • Mechanism geometry — spool radius, lever arm or linkage dimensions
  • Motor — model, loaded speed, shaft diameter and mounting interface if already selected
  • Required output speed — joint speed, spool speed or jaw motion
  • Available space — maximum gearhead diameter, body length and total motor + gearhead length
  • Duty cycle — continuous movement, short gripping events, hold time and rest time
  • Backlash / backdrivability target — if these affect control or human interaction
  • Feedback — motor encoder, output encoder or other position feedback if required

For a simple tendon spool, a first mechanical relation is:

output torque ≈ tendon force × spool radius

This is only a screening calculation. Friction, tendon routing, finger geometry, acceleration and transmission losses must also be considered in the real mechanism.

docs.title: If the Motor Is Already Selected
docs.text:
Do not choose a gearhead only by matching motor diameter.

Send:

  1. motor drawing or exact model
  2. loaded operating speed
  3. shaft diameter and usable shaft length
  4. mounting-hole pattern and locating pilot
  5. target output speed
  6. continuous / peak load
  7. available diameter and total assembly length

SigGear can then review the closest published frame and the motor-to-gearhead interface.

docs.text:

docs.title: About SigGear
docs.text:
Guangdong SigGear Drive Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. (brand: SigGear) is a custom gearbox and precision transmission manufacturer focused on custom engineering, prototype-to-production development, repeatable volume manufacturing and production delivery.

The standard planetary gearboxes, cycloidal reducers and robot joint actuators published on this site are public reference products. They are important evidence of SigGear's engineering and manufacturing capability, but they represent only the part of the company's work that can be shown publicly.

Many customer-specific transmission products, mechanisms and production programs cannot be disclosed because they are protected by confidentiality agreements. SigGear therefore uses reviewed standard products, public engineering documents, real manufacturing evidence and released test records to show capabilities without exposing confidential customer designs.

docs.title: Gear Manufacturing Capability
docs.text:
For precision transmission projects, the public equipment list is useful because it shows that SigGear's manufacturing environment includes dedicated gear-processing capability rather than only final assembly.

Process Publicly listed equipment Gear cutting Hobbing machine Gear shaping Gear shaping machine Gear finishing Gear grinding machine Additional gear / profile processing Gear turning / skiving-related equipment General precision machining CNC machining equipment

docs.text:
The official catalog also lists inspection and test equipment including:

These tools support dimensional, gear, performance and reliability-related verification depending on the project.

docs.title: Why This Matters When Qualifying a Custom Gearbox Manufacturer
docs.text:
For an OEM project, a supplier should be evaluated on more than a catalog drawing or finished assembly.

Relevant questions include:

  • Can the supplier process gears, not only assemble purchased parts?
  • Can the supplier measure the finished mechanical geometry?
  • Can gear mesh / backlash be checked?
  • Can torque, speed or life-related testing be planned where required?
  • Can the same engineering program move from prototype into repeat manufacturing?

SigGear's published equipment list and customization workflow provide public evidence for these company-level capabilities. The exact process route, inspection plan and test scope remain project-specific.

docs.title: Starting From a Customer Drawing, STEP Model or Physical Sample
docs.text:
SigGear can use customer geometry as the starting point for engineering review, while the manufacturing route is evaluated together with the real motor, load, speed, interfaces and production requirement.

docs.text: A custom transmission program may require several different kinds of manufacturing evidence:

docs.text:

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Examples:

docs.title: Durability / Environment

Examples:

These tests are project-specific and should not be assumed for every product without confirmation.

docs.title: Source-Backed Manufacturing Facts
docs.text:
This page collects publicly verifiable company-level manufacturing facts that help engineers, procurement teams and AI search systems understand SigGear's real operating scope.

It is intentionally separate from model-specific product claims.

docs.title: 1. Standard Products and Custom Products Are Both Part of SigGear
docs.text:
SigGear's official 2025 product catalog separates the business into:

  • standard products
  • non-standard customized products

The catalog states that customer-specific transmission work can run from R&D and design through sample / proofing and mass production.

Official source:

SigGear Product Catalog — 2025

This supports the public positioning used throughout the SigGear engineering site:

Standard products are public engineering reference platforms. Custom transmission development is a core part of the manufacturing business.

docs.title: 2. The Official Customization Process Includes Mass Production and Delivery
docs.text:
The same official catalog publishes a customization process that includes:

  1. requirement communication
  2. engineering / design work
  3. sample development
  4. sample production and internal testing
  5. small-batch trial production
  6. mass production and delivery

The catalog specifically states that detailed production planning can include material purchasing, production processes and process scheduling, followed by mass production after successful small-batch verification.

This is the strongest public source for SigGear's prototype → pilot → repeat production positioning.

Open the Official 2025 Catalog

docs.title: 3. Factory Scale: Current Public Source Is 20,000+ m²

A September 2025 company announcement also describes the new production base as covering 20,000 m².

Official sources:

docs.title: 8. Public Standard Products vs Confidential Customer Programs
docs.text:
SigGear publishes standard planetary gearboxes, cycloidal reducers and robot joint actuators because engineers need real products, specifications and STEP files to evaluate.

Many custom products cannot be shown publicly because they involve:

  • customer drawings
  • proprietary mechanisms
  • unreleased products
  • project-specific interfaces
  • future production programs
  • supplier relationships

The public catalog therefore shows part of SigGear's work, not the full scope of customer-specific transmission development.

docs.text:
The public SigGear catalog is not the full scope of the company's work. Many customer-specific products cannot be shown because the designs, mechanisms, interfaces and production programs are protected by confidentiality agreements.

SigGear's core capability is to take a transmission requirement from engineering review → prototype → design refinement → repeatable manufacturing, using standard products as public starting points where useful.

docs.title: Start With the Motion Problem, Not the Catalog
docs.text:
You do not need to know the gearbox ratio, gear structure or final motor before contacting SigGear.

You may already have a drawing and a complete specification. You may also have only:

  • a motor
  • a mechanism sketch
  • a target speed
  • a load or force requirement
  • an installation envelope
  • an early product concept

SigGear works with engineering teams on compact precision transmission problems using micro and miniature planetary gearboxes, cycloidal reducers, motors, motor + gearbox assemblies and integrated joint actuators.

The first step is to understand what the mechanism needs to do. From there, the transmission structure, ratio, motor interface and other design details can be evaluated.

Discuss Your Application Send Your Drawing or Concept

docs.text:
If an existing planetary gearbox is discontinued, failing in service or no longer fits the project requirement, SigGear can compare the current motor, ratio, interfaces, installation envelope and duty cycle against the nearest 8–42 mm platform.

An old sample, controlled drawing or failed-part photos can be more useful than a catalog listing when the goal is a close mechanical replacement.

docs.title: Cycloidal Transmission Engineering
docs.text:
For compact rotary joints and mechanisms where a cycloidal structure may be suitable, SigGear can review the required torque, speed, installation envelope, external loads and motor/control arrangement before selecting or modifying a platform.

docs.title: Motor + Gearbox Integration
docs.text:
A project does not need to start with a complete SigGear assembly.

Depending on the engineering requirement, the discussion can start from:

  • a customer's existing motor + SigGear gearbox
  • SigGear motor + SigGear gearbox
  • gearbox only
  • motor only
  • a matched motor + gearbox assembly
  • an integrated actuator where motor, reducer, sensing and control need to be evaluated together

For an existing motor, useful starting information includes the motor drawing, shaft dimensions, motor speed, available mounting space and the required output motion.

Motor + Gearbox Integration Engineering

docs.title: Robot Joint and Compact Actuator Development
docs.text:
For humanoid robots, quadruped robots, robotic arms, dexterous-hand mechanisms, exoskeletons and other compact robotic axes, the transmission may need to be evaluated together with the motor, encoder, driver, housing and mechanical interface.

SigGear's published joint actuators and cycloidal modules are reference products that show existing transmission structures and integration approaches. A new project does not need to use exactly the same dimensions or configuration.

docs.title: What Can Be Adjusted or Reviewed
docs.text:
The scope depends on the product family and engineering feasibility. Items that can be reviewed for applicable projects include:

Engineering area Examples Transmission planetary or cycloidal structure, stage count, reduction ratio Motor interface customer motor matching, motor shaft and mounting interface Packaging outer diameter, axial length, installation envelope Output output shaft, flange, mounting pattern and mechanical interface Mechanical integration housing, locating features and assembly arrangement Feedback / control encoder, driver, cable, connector and communication configuration where applicable Performance target torque, speed, backlash, external loads, duty cycle and operating condition

Final feasibility and specifications require engineering review. Not every parameter can be changed independently, and changing one requirement may affect torque, speed, size, efficiency, life, thermal behavior or cost.

docs.title: You Do Not Need a Complete Specification
docs.text:
Many projects start before the transmission parameters are fully defined.

If you do not know the reduction ratio, send the motor speed and desired output speed if available.

If you do not know the required torque, send the load, mechanism geometry, arm length, wheel size, screw / pulley information or another description of how the mechanism works.

If you are not sure whether planetary or cycloidal transmission is more suitable, send the application and installation constraints first.

A simple sketch, CAD screenshot or marked-up drawing is enough to start the first discussion.

docs.title: Typical Information for an Engineering Review
docs.text:
Send what you already know:

  • application and what needs to move
  • current motor or motor preference, if any
  • target output speed, if known
  • torque, load or force requirement, if known
  • maximum diameter, length or available installation space
  • shaft and mounting constraints
  • duty cycle or motion pattern
  • backlash, noise or positioning requirement where relevant
  • prototype quantity
  • expected production quantity, if known
  • drawing, CAD or mechanism sketch

Missing information can be identified during the engineering discussion.

docs.title: Engineering Development Path
docs.text:
A custom transmission project may move through the following steps:

Application / Concept → Feasibility Review → Transmission and Motor Evaluation → Drawing / Interface Review → Prototype or Sample → Testing → Parameter or Mechanical Refinement → Design Confirmation → Pilot Preparation → Production

The exact path depends on the project. An existing platform may only require interface changes, while another project may require a different transmission or motor arrangement.

SigGear does not treat a preliminary concept as a guaranteed final solution. The design is refined through engineering review, prototype manufacturing and testing where required.

Prototype → Design-In → Production

docs.title: Public Reference Products Are Evidence, Not the Limit of the Capability
docs.text:
Because many custom development projects are confidential, customer products and project details cannot always be shown publicly.

SigGear therefore uses reviewed standard and reference products to make its engineering and manufacturing capability visible.

Examples include:

Reference What an engineer can evaluate 32P Miniature Planetary Gearbox miniature planetary architecture, ratio / stage options, interface data, motor integration and public STEP SG-6010C Robot Joint Actuator integrated motor + planetary reducer + sensing / driver configuration and public mechanical resources CPM-80-25 Cycloidal Joint Module cycloidal joint architecture, mechanical interfaces, public CAD and measured performance data

docs.text:
Compact transmission engineering is used in many product categories, including:

Public Engineering Packs are used where reviewed data can be shared openly. They may include specifications, simplified STEP models, mechanical interfaces, integration guidance or measured test data.

Configuration-specific drawings and project details may remain controlled or confidential.

This allows engineers to evaluate SigGear's real products and technical approach without exposing confidential customer designs.

docs.title: Start From the Joint Requirement, Not the Transmission Assumption
docs.text:
You do not need to decide in advance that the project must use a cycloidal reducer.

For a compact robot joint, actuator or rotary mechanism, the first engineering review should start from the actual requirements:

  • continuous and peak torque
  • required output speed
  • installation diameter and axial length
  • load direction and external loads
  • motor or motor constraints
  • duty cycle
  • backlash / positioning requirement
  • driver, encoder and communication needs
  • prototype and expected production quantity

SigGear can review these inputs and determine whether an existing cycloidal platform, a modified cycloidal configuration, a planetary solution or another arrangement should be evaluated.

Send Your Joint Requirement Request Engineering Review

docs.title: When a Cycloidal Structure May Be Worth Evaluating
docs.text:
A cycloidal transmission may be considered when a project needs a compact rotary joint with a relatively high torque requirement, limited axial space, controlled backlash and a mechanical architecture that can accommodate the selected cycloidal platform.

This does not mean that cycloidal transmission is always the better choice. Final suitability depends on the complete operating condition, including:

  • torque-speed cycle
  • peak duration
  • installation envelope
  • radial and axial loads
  • efficiency requirement
  • thermal condition
  • noise requirement
  • motor and controller selection
  • shock or impact loading
  • required service life

For projects where these trade-offs are still unclear, the engineering review should compare the actual application requirements rather than choosing the transmission type from a general rule.

docs.title: The current catalog joint does not fit
docs.text:
The project may require a different:

  • outer diameter
  • axial thickness
  • mounting pattern
  • locating feature
  • output interface
  • rear housing
  • cable or connector arrangement
  • driver / encoder configuration

The first step is to identify which requirements are fixed and which can be adjusted.

docs.title: The motor or controller is already selected
docs.text:
A project may start from a customer-selected motor, driver or control architecture.

In that case, useful starting information includes:

  • motor drawing and dimensions
  • operating voltage
  • motor speed
  • current / power information
  • shaft and mounting interface
  • driver type
  • encoder or sensor requirement
  • communication interface
  • available total assembly space

The motor, reducer and interface need to be reviewed as one system rather than as independent parts.

docs.title: The customer needs the reducer or mechanical module only
docs.text:
Some projects use the customer's own motor, encoder or controller. Others require an integrated motor + reducer + driver configuration.

The exact supply scope depends on the selected platform and project requirements and must be confirmed during engineering review.

docs.title: The torque requirement is known but the architecture is not
docs.text:
If you know the output torque, speed and available space but are not sure whether to use a planetary or cycloidal structure, send those conditions first.

SigGear can compare the available reference platforms and identify what needs to be calculated or tested before the transmission structure is fixed.

docs.title: Existing SigGear Cycloidal Reference Platforms
docs.text:
SigGear currently publishes several cycloidal joint-module reference products.

Reference model Published transmission Published reference data CPM-80-25 Cycloidal pinwheel, 25:1 80 mm OD, 10 Nm rated torque, 50 Nm peak torque, 120 rpm rated output speed CPM-100-25 Cycloidal pinwheel, 25:1 100 mm OD, 25 Nm rated torque, 75 Nm peak torque, 60 rpm rated output speed CPM-78-39 Cycloidal pinwheel, 39:1 78.7 mm OD, 20 Nm rated torque, 52 Nm peak torque, 48 rpm rated output speed

These values belong to the published reference models only. They must not be transferred to a new diameter, ratio, motor or custom configuration without engineering confirmation.

docs.title: CPM-80-25 as a Public Engineering Reference
docs.text:
CPM-80-25 currently has the most complete public cycloidal Engineering Pack on the SigGear site.

Public resources include:

  • technical datasheet
  • mechanical-interface reference
  • simplified STEP for the no-driver configuration
  • simplified STEP for the integrated-driver reference configuration
  • measured performance data

View CPM-80-25 View CPM-80-25 Datasheet View Mechanical Interface View Measured Performance Data

The measured performance page contains test points at 24 V, 36 V and 48 V. These measured points are engineering evidence from the released test source and must not be treated as universal continuous operating ratings for a different configuration.

The public rated output torque for CPM-80-25 remains 10 Nm, with 50 Nm published peak output torque for preliminary product selection. Peak duration and application suitability require review of the actual current limit, duty cycle, thermal condition and installation.

docs.title: What Can Be Reviewed for a Custom Project
docs.text:
Depending on the reference platform and engineering feasibility, the following areas may be reviewed:

Engineering area Examples Transmission ratio and cycloidal structure based on the selected platform Motor integration motor size, speed, shaft, mounting and electrical constraints Packaging outer diameter, axial thickness, housing and installation envelope Output interface mounting pattern, flange, locating feature and customer-side mechanical interface Feedback / control Hall / encoder / driver configuration where supported by the selected platform Communication CAN or RS485 where supported by the selected driver configuration Performance target torque, speed, backlash, external loads and duty cycle Assembly cable, connector and rear-housing arrangement where applicable

Not every item can be modified independently. A requested change may affect size, torque, speed, efficiency, life, thermal behavior, control hardware or cost.

docs.title: Integrated Driver or External Driver?
docs.text:
The SigGear cycloidal reference products do not all use the same electronics.

For example:

  • CPM-80-25 can be supplied with or without an integrated driver, with driver / encoder / communication details confirmed for the selected configuration.
  • CPM-100-25 can be supplied with or without an integrated driver, with the final driver / encoder / connector arrangement confirmed in the quotation.
  • CPM-78-39 uses Hall sensors in its standard catalog configuration and does not include an integrated driver or absolute encoder as a standard claim.

Do not assume CAN, RS485, absolute encoder or closed-loop control across all cycloidal models. The electronics must be matched to the quoted configuration.

docs.title: What to Send First
docs.text:
A complete specification is not required for the first discussion.

Start with the information you already have:

  1. Application — robot joint, actuator or other rotary mechanism
  2. Torque — continuous and peak requirement if known
  3. Peak duration — if a peak torque is important
  4. Speed — required output speed
  5. Installation space — maximum diameter and axial length
  6. External loads — radial / axial / impact conditions if relevant
  7. Motor / controller — existing motor or preferred electrical architecture
  8. Interface — mounting, shaft, flange or drawing if already defined
  9. Project stage — concept, prototype, pilot or production planning
  10. Quantity — prototype quantity and expected production volume if known

If torque is not yet defined, send the mechanism geometry, load, arm length or other information that describes the joint.

If the transmission type is not yet defined, send the operating conditions and let the engineering review start from the application.

docs.title: Engineering Development Path
docs.text:
A custom cycloidal project may move through:

Application / Joint Requirement → Feasibility Review → Cycloidal vs. Alternative Transmission Evaluation → Motor / Interface Review → Configuration Drawing → Prototype or Sample → Mechanical / Electrical Test → Parameter or Interface Refinement → Design Confirmation → Pilot Preparation → Production

The exact sequence depends on the maturity of the customer's design and how much of the motor, control and mechanical architecture has already been fixed.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
Cycloidal transmission may be evaluated for compact rotary joints and mechanisms in areas such as:

  • humanoid robots
  • quadruped robots
  • robotic arms
  • exoskeletons
  • rehabilitation robots
  • compact industrial rotary axes
  • other mechanisms requiring a compact high-torque joint drive

These are application areas where cycloidal transmission may be relevant. They are not statements that SigGear has a public customer case in every listed application.

SigGear uses public reference products, CAD resources, interface drawings and measured test data to demonstrate real engineering capability without exposing confidential customer designs.

docs.title: Custom Gearbox Manufacturer From Customer Drawing, STEP or Physical Sample
docs.text: A custom transmission project does not need to begin with a SigGear catalog model.

docs.title: “Here Is Our Drawing / STEP / Sample. Can SigGear Review and Manufacture It?”
docs.text:
Yes. SigGear can start a custom gearbox or precision transmission review from a customer drawing, STEP model, mechanism layout, existing assembly or physical sample.

The first step is not to copy visible dimensions blindly. SigGear reviews the geometry together with the real motor, speed, load, duty cycle, interfaces and production requirement before a prototype or manufacturing configuration is confirmed.

A project can continue from:

Drawing / STEP / Sample → Engineering Review → Prototype → Application Validation → Design Refinement → Design Freeze → Pilot / Repeat Production

Send Drawing / STEP for Engineering Review Manufacturing Equipment & Inspection Prototype → Volume Production

docs.title: What You Can Send
docs.text:
Useful starting files or evidence include:

  • 2D mechanical drawing
  • STEP model
  • assembly drawing
  • mechanism sketch
  • marked-up screenshot
  • motor drawing
  • old gearbox drawing or datasheet
  • physical sample information
  • photographs of the installed mechanism
  • photographs of failed or worn components where relevant

A complete gearbox specification is not required before the first review.

docs.title: What SigGear Can Manufacture or Modify From a Customer Drawing
docs.text:
Depending on engineering feasibility, the project may involve:

  • custom planetary gearbox
  • custom cycloidal reducer
  • motor + gearbox assembly
  • modified reduction ratio
  • custom input pinion / shaft
  • custom output shaft / flange
  • housing or mounting modification
  • customer-motor interface
  • bearing / external-load arrangement
  • encoder, driver, cable or connector integration where applicable
  • prototype and repeat-production configuration

A drawing or STEP model defines geometry. It does not by itself establish the correct torque rating, material, heat treatment, bearing arrangement, service life or production process.

docs.title: What SigGear Reviews From the Drawing
docs.text:
The engineering review may include:

Area What to check Installation envelope Maximum diameter, axial length and total assembly space Motor interface Shaft, pilot, mounting holes, pinion / input feature and operating speed Output interface Shaft, flange, key, bolt pattern and locating features Motion target Required output speed, ratio and direction Load Continuous torque, peak torque, radial / axial loads and duty cycle Transmission structure Planetary, cycloidal or another feasible compact arrangement Precision Backlash, positioning or repeatability requirement where applicable Electronics Encoder, driver, cable, connector and communication where applicable Production Prototype quantity, forecast, inspection requirements and target schedule

The drawing defines geometry. It does not automatically define the correct material, heat treatment, bearing arrangement, ratio or operating rating.

Replacing an existing gearbox rather than developing a new mechanism? Use the Existing Gearbox Replacement & Redesign path when the motor, mounting pattern or machine interface must remain unchanged.

docs.title: If You Only Have a Physical Sample — No Complete Drawing
docs.text:
A sample can be useful when the original drawing is missing or incomplete.

The review may need to identify:

  • overall dimensions
  • motor-side interface
  • output interface
  • stage arrangement
  • ratio if it can be established
  • gear and shaft geometry
  • bearing arrangement
  • visible wear / failure evidence
  • installation constraints

A worn sample must be interpreted carefully because the measured geometry may no longer represent the original design condition.

Replacement / Failure Review

docs.title: If the Drawing Must Remain Confidential
docs.text:
Many customer drawings relate to unreleased products or proprietary mechanisms.

You can begin with non-sensitive information such as:

  • application category
  • required torque / speed
  • maximum envelope
  • motor type
  • prototype quantity
  • expected production volume
  • NDA requirement

Detailed drawings can be exchanged after the appropriate confidentiality process is agreed.

SigGear does not publish confidential customer STEP models / drawings or customer-specific products as public case studies.

docs.title: What to Send for the First Review
docs.text:
A useful first package can be very small:

  1. drawing / STEP model / photos / physical sample
  2. motor model or drawing, if already selected
  3. loaded motor speed
  4. required output speed or ratio

docs.title: Custom Shaft, Mounting, Ratio and Interface Requests
docs.text:
Depending on the selected gearbox platform and engineering feasibility, project-specific review may include:

  • reduction ratio

  • motor shaft and input interface
  • output shaft shape and length
  • mounting flange or mounting pattern
  • housing and installation structure
  • encoder or brake integration where applicable
  • cable and connector configuration where applicable
  • backlash target
  • radial and axial load conditions
  • duty cycle and operating condition

Changing one requirement may affect other parameters such as torque, speed, efficiency, size, service life, thermal behavior or cost. Final feasibility must therefore be confirmed as a complete configuration rather than one parameter at a time.

A custom shaft or mounting request is not automatically feasible on every 8–42 mm frame. The practical starting point is to compare the nearest standard platform, then review the output shaft, motor-side interface, flange, stage count and available axial envelope together.

docs.title: I Know the Output Speed but Not the Gear Ratio
docs.text:
The exact ratio does not need to be defined before the first discussion.

If the motor speed and desired output speed are known, they provide a starting point for ratio selection:

preliminary reduction ratio ≈ motor speed / desired output speed

The final configuration still needs to account for the available stage ratios, torque requirement, gearbox input-speed limit, efficiency, duty cycle and motor operating point.

If the motor speed is not yet fixed, send the application and target output motion first.

docs.title: I Do Not Know the Required Torque
docs.text:

  • pulley or screw information
  • friction or resistance that must be overcome
  • acceleration requirement
  • motion cycle
  • whether the axis works against gravity
  • a sketch or CAD screenshot of the mechanism

The engineering review can then identify what needs to be calculated, estimated or tested before selecting the gearbox.

docs.title: Typical Project Situations
docs.text: Custom planetary gearhead engineering may be relevant when:

docs.title: The motor is already fixed
docs.text: The gearbox must be adapted around an existing motor shaft, pilot, mounting pattern, speed and available assembly length.

docs.title: The gearbox must fit an existing mechanism
docs.text: The project has a fixed diameter, length, mounting surface or output location that a catalog configuration does not match directly.

docs.title: The output shaft is application-specific
docs.text: The project requires a different shaft geometry, shaft length, flange or mounting arrangement.

docs.title: The output speed is known but the transmission is not
docs.text: The engineer knows how fast the mechanism should move but has not selected the stage count or ratio.

docs.title: The product needs a motor + gearbox assembly
docs.text: The project needs the motor and gearbox evaluated together instead of sourcing the two parts separately.

docs.title: The project is moving from prototype toward production
docs.text: A preliminary gearbox configuration needs to be refined around the actual motor, housing, loads, mounting and operating cycle before the design is frozen.

docs.title: Engineering Review Path
docs.text:
A typical custom planetary gearhead project can move through:

Application / Existing Motor / Drawing → Feasibility Review → Frame Size and Ratio Evaluation → Motor and Interface Review → Configuration Drawing → Prototype or Sample → Application Test → Parameter / Interface Refinement → Design Confirmation → Pilot Preparation → Production

The exact sequence depends on how mature the customer's design already is.

docs.title: What to Send First
docs.text:
You do not need to prepare a long specification sheet before contacting SigGear.

Start with the information you already have:

  1. Application — what the mechanism needs to do
  2. Motor — drawing or motor model if one has already been selected
  3. Output target — speed and torque / load if known
  4. Space — maximum diameter, length or installation envelope
  5. Interface — shaft, mounting or drawing if these are already defined
  6. Project stage — concept, prototype, pilot or production planning
  7. Quantity — prototype quantity and expected production volume if known

If some of these are unknown, send the drawing, mechanism or product concept first. The missing engineering inputs can be identified during the review.

docs.text:

  • electric curtains and smart-home mechanisms

  • other products that require a small motor and reduction gearbox

These are application areas where planetary transmission may be relevant. They are not statements that SigGear has a public customer case in every listed application.

docs.title: The Public Catalog Is Only the Visible Part of SigGear
docs.text:
SigGear's public planetary gearboxes, cycloidal reducers and robot joint actuators are important engineering references, but they are not the full scope of the company's work.

Many customer-specific transmission projects cannot be published because they involve confidential drawings, unreleased products, proprietary mechanisms, application details or future production programs protected by confidentiality agreements.

For that reason, the standard products on this site should be understood as:

  • real products that engineers can evaluate publicly
  • evidence of transmission architectures and manufacturing capability
  • starting platforms for modified or custom projects
  • public design-in resources with datasheets, drawings and STEP files where released

They should not be treated as the limit of SigGear's engineering or manufacturing capability.

docs.title: SigGear's Core Strength: Custom Engineering That Can Move Into Production
docs.text:
SigGear works with customers that need the transmission to fit the product, rather than forcing the product to fit a catalog gearbox. Customer drawings, STEP models, existing motors, failed gearboxes and physical samples can all be valid starting points for engineering review.

A project can start from:

  • a motor that is already selected
  • an existing gearbox that needs replacement
  • a customer drawing or STEP model
  • a mechanism with limited installation space
  • a target speed, torque or motion requirement
  • a robot joint concept
  • a prototype that needs a different ratio, shaft, flange or housing
  • a production product that needs a repeatable custom transmission

Depending on the project, engineering review can include:

Area Examples Transmission planetary or cycloidal architecture, stage count, reduction ratio Motor integration customer motor, SigGear motor, shaft / pinion, pilot and mounting pattern Packaging diameter, axial length, housing and installation envelope Output interface shaft, flange, key, mounting pattern and locating features Bearing / loads radial, axial and overturning-load arrangement Feedback / control encoder, Hall, driver, cable, connector and communication where applicable Production drawing control, configuration freeze, inspection points, pilot and repeat manufacturing

Not every requested change is feasible on every platform. Final specifications require engineering review and, where necessary, prototype validation.

docs.title: Can SigGear develop a gearbox from my motor?
docs.text: Yes, the review can start from an existing motor drawing and operating point. The shaft, pilot, mounting pattern, motor speed, required output speed, load and installation envelope are reviewed together before a gearbox configuration is confirmed.

docs.title: Can SigGear work from my drawing or STEP model?
docs.text: Yes. A customer 2D drawing, STEP model, mechanism layout or physical sample can be used as a starting point. The drawing defines geometry, while the engineering review also needs operating load, speed, duty cycle and production requirements.

docs.title: Can SigGear review a gearbox that keeps failing?
docs.text: Yes. The review should include the failed unit or drawings, motor, operating condition, duty cycle and failure evidence such as gear wear, bearing damage, overheating, backlash growth or abnormal noise. The objective is to understand the failure before evaluating a replacement or redesign.

docs.title: Can a project start with prototypes and later move to volume production?
docs.text: Yes. For applicable projects, SigGear can support the path from prototype and application testing through design refinement, design freeze, pilot preparation and repeatable manufacturing. Prototype quantity, forecast and target schedule help plan the development path.

docs.title: Can SigGear work under NDA?
docs.text: Yes, confidential projects can be discussed without publishing the customer design. Detailed drawings and proprietary files should be exchanged only after the appropriate confidentiality process is agreed.

docs.title: Are SigGear's public standard products the full product range?
docs.text: No. The published planetary gearboxes, cycloidal modules and robot joint actuators are public reference platforms. Many customer-specific products and production programs cannot be shown publicly because they are confidential.

docs.title: From Prototype to Repeatable Volume Manufacturing
docs.text:
SigGear's role does not need to end after a prototype works.

For applicable customer programs, the development path can continue through:

Requirement / Existing Design → Feasibility Review → Preliminary Configuration → Prototype / Sample → Application Test → Design Refinement → Design Freeze → Pilot Preparation → Repeatable Volume Manufacturing

The purpose of this process is to convert a custom engineering solution into a configuration that can be manufactured and inspected repeatedly.

docs.title: Volume Production and Delivery Capability
docs.text:
A key part of SigGear's manufacturing value is the ability to support volume production, not only one-off prototypes.

After the configuration is frozen, production planning can cover:

  • repeat batch manufacturing
  • component machining and gear processing
  • assembly planning
  • inspection and outgoing verification
  • material / component preparation
  • production scheduling
  • packaging requirements
  • batch delivery planning

SigGear also works to support short production lead times for volume programs where the configuration, demand and production plan allow it.

Actual lead time is project-specific. It depends on quantity, customization scope, materials, tooling, controlled drawings, inspection requirements and production scheduling, so SigGear does not publish one universal delivery-time promise for every custom project.

docs.title: “Our Current Gearbox Keeps Failing. Can SigGear Review It?”
docs.text:
Yes. A gearbox failure review can start from the failed unit, old drawing, STEP model, worn-part photos, motor information or the operating condition already available.

A gearbox that keeps failing should not be replaced from the model number alone.

The first question is:

What is actually failing, under what operating condition, and which parts of the existing design must remain unchanged?

SigGear can review a failed planetary gearbox or compact reducer as an engineering project when the customer can provide the unit, drawing, photographs, motor information, operating condition or other failure evidence.

This is an engineering review path, not a promise that every failure can be solved by one material or geometry change.

Start a Failure / Durability Review Existing Gearbox Replacement / Redesign

docs.title: Typical Failure Symptoms to Document
docs.text:
Useful observations can include:

  • gear tooth wear
  • pitting or surface damage
  • chipped or broken teeth
  • worn sun gear, planet gear or ring gear
  • carrier or pin damage
  • bearing damage
  • shaft damage
  • increasing backlash over time
  • abnormal noise or vibration
  • overheating
  • lubricant contamination or loss
  • reduced output torque
  • intermittent jamming
  • failure after a repeatable number of cycles

A symptom does not by itself identify the root cause.

For example, tooth wear may relate to load, material, heat treatment, gear geometry, lubrication, alignment, duty cycle, speed, shock load, contamination or several factors together.

docs.title: What to Send
docs.text:
For a useful first review, provide whatever is available:

  1. failed gearbox / reducer model
  2. physical sample, if available
  3. old drawing or STEP model
  4. photos of worn or broken components
  5. motor model and drawing
  6. loaded motor speed
  7. required output speed / ratio
  8. continuous and peak load
  9. duty cycle and peak duration
  10. approximate operating hours or cycles before failure
  11. radial / axial load, if applied
  12. operating environment, if relevant
  13. what must remain unchanged — motor, envelope, shaft, mounting or ratio
  14. prototype quantity and expected production volume

If detailed files are confidential, the first discussion can begin with non-sensitive dimensions, operating conditions and failure symptoms.

docs.title: What the Engineering Review May Examine
docs.text:
Depending on the evidence and the design, possible review areas include:

Area Questions Gear geometry Is the stage / tooth geometry appropriate for the actual load and ratio? Tooth width Is available face width compatible with the load path and packaging? Materials Does the selected material match the intended duty and manufacturing route? Heat treatment Does the application require a different confirmed heat-treatment approach? Stage arrangement Is the load distributed appropriately across the reduction stages? Bearings Are output / internal bearings suitable for the actual radial, axial and overturning loads? Shaft / carrier Are interfaces and supporting structures contributing to stress or misalignment? Lubrication Are lubricant type, amount, retention and operating condition appropriate? Speed Does the real motor operating point differ from the original design assumption? Duty cycle Are continuous, peak, reversal and holding conditions represented correctly? Assembly Are alignment, preload, fits or assembly conditions relevant? Environment Temperature, contamination or other external conditions where applicable

The review should be based on project evidence. SigGear does not infer a material, treatment or lifetime claim from photographs alone.

docs.title: Keep the Motor — Redesign the Transmission
docs.text:
Many replacement projects need to keep the existing motor, electronics and machine interfaces.

In that case the redesigned transmission may need to preserve:

  • motor shaft
  • locating pilot
  • mounting-hole pattern
  • total diameter
  • total assembly length
  • output shaft / flange
  • output speed
  • customer mounting interface

while changing one or more internal transmission details.

docs.text:

A useful initial package can be as simple as:

  • the motor model / drawing and loaded operating speed
  • the required output speed or ratio

  • approximate hours or cycles before failure

  • prototype quantity and expected production volume

docs.text:
A practical development path can be:

Failed Unit / Evidence → Operating-Condition Review → Interface Measurement / Drawing Review → Preliminary Redesign → Prototype → Representative Load / Duty Testing → Design Refinement

The prototype should be tested against the failure mode that matters to the application rather than only checked for mechanical fit.

docs.title: Manufacturing and Inspection Evidence
docs.text:
A durability redesign is only useful if the revised transmission can be manufactured and inspected repeatably.

SigGear publishes company-level evidence for gear-processing, dimensional-inspection and test resources including gear hobbing, gear shaping, gear grinding, CNC machining, CMM, gear testing, backlash inspection, dynamometer and life-test capability.

If the replacement is intended for an ongoing product, production requirements should be considered before the redesign is frozen.

That can include:

  • material / process definition where applicable

SigGear does not automatically claim:

docs.title: 8P–42P Existing-Motor Design-In Workflow
docs.text:
For an existing motor, SigGear does not start by assuming a standard motor adapter. The first review narrows five engineering gates:

  1. Frame / envelope — available gearbox diameter, stage-dependent gearbox length and maximum total assembly length.
  2. Motor operating point — actual motor speed, power and duty cycle against the selected gearbox input-speed and load limits.
  3. Output target — required output speed or preliminary ratio, continuous load and short-duration peak load.
  4. Mechanical interface — motor shaft diameter and usable length, shaft feature, locating pilot, mounting-hole pattern and the required gearbox input arrangement.
  5. Design-In release — use the public STEP for preliminary packaging, then confirm the selected stage / ratio / motor interface before controlled configuration STEP / drawing release.

A frame-size match does not prove motor compatibility. The motor and gearbox interface must be reviewed for the exact project.

docs.text: Real compact geared motor assemblies photographed at SigGear with a ruler for scale. Exact motor, gearbox, output shaft and wiring configurations vary by project.

docs.title: Path A — I Already Have a Motor
docs.text:
If the motor is already fixed, the first task is to determine whether the gearbox can be matched mechanically and whether the motor operating point is suitable for the required output.

Useful information includes:

  • motor drawing or exact motor model
  • motor type
  • nominal voltage
  • rated and peak power, if available
  • rated and no-load speed
  • shaft diameter and usable shaft length
  • shaft flat, key, pinion or other input feature
  • motor mounting-hole pattern
  • locating pilot diameter
  • maximum total assembly length
  • required output speed
  • required continuous and peak torque, or the load if torque is not yet known
  • duty cycle
  • expected prototype and production quantity

A motor drawing is often more useful than a long text description because it makes the shaft, pilot and mounting constraints visible immediately.

docs.title: Path B — I Need a Complete Motor + Gearbox Solution
docs.text:
If the motor has not yet been selected, start from the output requirement and installation envelope.

Useful starting inputs are:

  • application and what needs to move
  • required output speed
  • continuous and peak torque, load or force if known
  • available diameter and total length
  • operating voltage or available power supply
  • duty cycle and motion pattern
  • noise, backlash or positioning requirement where relevant
  • shaft and mounting requirements
  • encoder, brake, cable or connector requirements where relevant
  • prototype quantity and expected production volume

The motor and gearbox should be evaluated together. A high motor speed may reduce required motor torque but can increase reduction-ratio and gearbox input-speed requirements. A different ratio can change output speed, available torque, efficiency and gearbox length.

Final selection therefore requires review of the complete operating point rather than only one parameter.

docs.title: If the Gear Ratio Is Unknown
docs.text:
The customer does not need to calculate the final ratio before contacting SigGear.

When motor speed and desired output speed are known, a preliminary ratio can be estimated from:

preliminary reduction ratio ≈ motor speed / desired output speed

The final ratio still needs to be checked against:

  • available gearbox ratios and stage count
  • gearbox input-speed limit
  • required output torque
  • motor operating point
  • gearbox efficiency
  • duty cycle
  • assembly length
  • thermal condition

If the motor speed is also unknown, send the application and output motion requirement first.

docs.title: If the Required Torque Is Unknown
docs.text:
A project can start from the mechanism.

Useful information can include:

  • load or payload
  • arm length or linkage geometry
  • wheel diameter
  • pulley, belt, screw or rack information
  • friction or resistance
  • acceleration requirement
  • gravity direction
  • motion cycle
  • a sketch, STEP model or marked-up drawing

From this information, the engineering review can identify what must be calculated, measured or tested before final motor and gearbox selection.

docs.title: Mechanical Matching Between Motor and Gearbox
docs.text:
The motor-to-gearbox interface normally needs review of:

  • motor shaft diameter
  • usable shaft length
  • shaft geometry
  • gearbox input interface
  • mounting-hole pattern
  • locating pilot
  • concentricity and assembly arrangement
  • total axial length
  • torque-transfer method
  • available housing space

A motor that is suitable electrically may still require a different mechanical interface before it can be used with a gearbox platform.

docs.title: Motor Types and Product Families
docs.text:
SigGear's current public micro gear-motor information states that, depending on the selected gearbox and project requirements, engineering review can include:

  • brushed DC motors
  • brushless DC motors
  • stepper motors
  • servo motors
  • customer-specified motors

Compatibility is not assumed from motor type alone. Input speed, power, shaft interface, duty cycle, thermal conditions and required output performance must be reviewed for the selected gearbox.

Browse Micro Gear Motors Browse Planetary Gearboxes

docs.title: Existing SigGear Planetary Platforms
docs.text:
For miniature and compact motor + gearbox projects, SigGear publishes planetary gearbox platforms from 8 mm to 42 mm nominal outer diameter.

The current public series includes:

8P / 10P / 12P / 14P / 16P / 20P / 22P / 24P / 28P / 32P / 36P / 42P

Each frame size has its own stage count, ratio, torque, efficiency, length and operating limits. Data from one frame size must not be transferred to another without confirmation.

docs.text:
The 32P Engineering Pack currently provides the clearest public example of SigGear's motor-to-gearbox integration workflow.

For the published 32P reference:

docs.title: Other Compact Drive Architectures
docs.text:
Not every motorized project should use a miniature planetary gearbox.

Depending on torque, space, joint architecture, load condition and control requirements, SigGear may also review:

  • cycloidal transmission
  • integrated robot joint actuators
  • flat BLDC motor and joint-drive configurations
  • other compact transmission arrangements supported by the available engineering platforms

docs.title: Typical Project Situations
docs.text: Motor + gearbox integration may be relevant when:

docs.title: A customer motor must be retained
docs.text: The gearbox must be designed or selected around the existing shaft, pilot, mounting pattern, speed and assembly envelope.

docs.title: A standard gear motor is too large
docs.text: The project needs a shorter, smaller-diameter or differently arranged assembly.

docs.title: The output shaft or mounting is application-specific
docs.text: The customer needs a different shaft, flange, mounting pattern or housing interface.

docs.title: The team knows the final motion but not the motor
docs.text: The output speed, load and space are known, but the motor and reduction ratio are still open.

docs.title: Prototype performance needs refinement
docs.text: The first sample moves, but output speed, torque, noise, temperature, current or mechanical fit needs to be adjusted before design freeze.

docs.title: Engineering Development Path
docs.text:
A motor + gearbox project may move through:

Application / Motor / Drawing → Feasibility Review → Motor and Gearbox Operating-Point Review → Ratio and Frame-Size Evaluation → Mechanical Interface Review → Configuration Drawing → Prototype / Sample → Application Test → Motor / Ratio / Interface Refinement → Design Confirmation → Pilot Preparation → Production

The exact path depends on whether the motor, gearbox, mechanism and electrical architecture are already fixed.

docs.title: What to Send First
docs.text:
For a first review, send what you already have.

If you already have a motor:

  1. motor drawing or model
  2. motor speed
  3. required output speed
  4. load or torque requirement
  5. maximum assembly size
  6. shaft / mounting constraints

If you need a complete motor + gearbox:

  1. application
  2. output speed
  3. load / torque if known
  4. available diameter and length
  5. operating voltage
  6. duty cycle
  7. prototype and expected production quantity

A complete specification is not required before the first discussion.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text:
Compact motor + gearbox integration can be relevant in:

  • humanoid and service robots
  • quadruped robots
  • robotic arms
  • dexterous hands and grippers
  • exoskeletons
  • UAV and drone mechanisms
  • AGV / AMR
  • robotic lawn and outdoor equipment
  • electric curtains and smart-home mechanisms
  • smart sanitary and household mechanisms
  • medical and laboratory equipment
  • precision instruments
  • compact industrial automation
  • other products that require a small motor and reduction transmission

These are application areas where a compact drive may be relevant. They are not statements that SigGear has a public production case in every listed application.

docs.title: Confidential Development Projects
docs.text:
Custom motor + gearbox development often involves customer drawings, unreleased products and application-specific interfaces.

Those projects may not be publicly shown.

SigGear therefore uses public gearbox platforms, motor-integration references, CAD, interface data and test resources to help new engineering teams evaluate its capabilities without exposing confidential customer designs.

docs.title: OEM Gearbox Volume Manufacturing & Delivery Planning
docs.text:
A custom gearbox project is commercially useful only if the validated design can be manufactured repeatedly.

SigGear's role can continue beyond prototype development into repeatable batch / volume manufacturing and production delivery planning for applicable custom transmission programs.

This page describes the manufacturing path and planning information required. It does not publish one universal production capacity or guaranteed lead time for every product.

Discuss a Prototype-to-Volume Project Prototype → Volume Production

docs.title: Start Production Planning Before the Prototype Is Final
docs.text:
If a project may later require hundreds or thousands of units, the production requirement should be discussed early.

Useful planning inputs include:

  • prototype quantity
  • expected pilot quantity
  • estimated annual volume
  • expected batch size
  • target prototype date
  • target pilot date
  • target production date
  • required delivery destination
  • packaging / labeling requirements
  • inspection or documentation requirements
  • forecast stability
  • whether the product is expected to change after prototype testing

These inputs do not lock the customer into a purchase. They help determine whether the engineering path should be planned as a future production program.

docs.title: The Transition From Prototype to Production
docs.text:
A typical path is:

Engineering Requirement → Prototype / Sample → Application Validation → Design Refinement → Design Freeze → Controlled Configuration → Pilot Preparation → Repeatable Batch Manufacturing → Production Delivery

A prototype that moves correctly is not automatically production-ready.

Before repeat manufacturing, the project may need to confirm:

  • final ratio
  • motor and motor interface
  • output shaft / flange
  • housing / mounting
  • bearings and external-load assumptions
  • materials / process route where applicable
  • drawing revision
  • inspection requirements
  • electronics / cable / connector configuration where applicable
  • packaging and identification

docs.title: What Repeatable Manufacturing Requires
docs.text:
For a custom transmission, repeat production depends on controlling the configuration.

That can include:

Production area Typical requirement Drawings controlled product / interface revision Components repeatable machining and gear processing Assembly defined configuration and assembly requirements Inspection agreed dimensional / functional checks Incoming materials confirmed materials / purchased components where applicable Testing project-specific verification where required Packaging agreed product protection, labels and batch identification Scheduling quantity, batch plan and target delivery window

The exact process depends on the product and customer requirement.

docs.title: SigGear Manufacturing Evidence
docs.text:
SigGear publishes real photographs from its manufacturing environment covering:

  • precision machining
  • gear processing
  • assembly workstations
  • quality inspection

The company also publishes separate testing and metrology evidence.

Manufacturing & Quality Evidence Manufacturing Equipment & Inspection Capability Testing, Metrology & Validation Evidence

These photographs are evidence of real manufacturing and inspection activity. They do not quantify a universal monthly capacity, cycle time or lead time.

docs.title: Short Production Lead Times — What Can Be Said Responsibly
docs.text:
SigGear works to support short production lead times for applicable volume programs when the configuration, materials, quantity, inspection requirements and production plan allow it.

Actual delivery timing is project-specific.

Important variables include:

  • customization scope
  • final quantity
  • material availability
  • purchased components
  • tooling
  • heat treatment / external processes where applicable
  • inspection requirement
  • assembly complexity
  • design changes
  • production scheduling
  • delivery destination

For that reason, the correct process is to review the target schedule with the exact configuration rather than publish a generic “fast delivery” promise.

docs.title: What Helps a Time-Sensitive Program
docs.text:
A customer can help production planning by providing:

  • a stable forecast
  • expected batch quantities
  • target launch date
  • required delivery cadence
  • early notification of design changes
  • drawing / configuration approval timing
  • critical inspection requirements
  • packaging / labeling requirements

When timing is important, include the target schedule in the first engineering brief.

Start Prototype-to-Volume Review

docs.title: Confidential Production Programs
docs.text:
Many volume programs involve unreleased customer products, confidential drawings or supplier information.

SigGear does not use confidential production programs as public case studies.

Public evidence therefore focuses on:

  • released standard products
  • real manufacturing scenes
  • engineering documentation
  • testing / inspection resources
  • public custom-engineering workflows

This allows customers and AI search systems to understand the manufacturing capability without exposing customer projects.

docs.title: Public Reference Products vs Production Programs
docs.text:
The 8–42 mm planetary gearheads, robot joint actuators and cycloidal modules on this site are public reference products.

A production program may:

  • use a standard product
  • modify a standard platform
  • integrate a customer motor
  • use a project-specific shaft / flange / housing
  • require a custom ratio or interface
  • require a customer-specific actuator configuration

The public catalog is therefore a starting point, not the limit of the manufacturing scope.

docs.title: Start a Volume Manufacturing Review
docs.text:
For a meaningful first discussion, send:

  • application
  • drawing / CAD if available
  • prototype quantity
  • estimated annual volume
  • target schedule
  • delivery destination
  • current design stage
  • NDA requirement
  • technical requirements already known

Wanrong Wang International Sales / Sales Engineer, SigGear wangwanrong@siggear.com

Discuss Prototype → Volume Production

docs.title: Custom Gearbox & Transmission: Prototype to Volume Production
“We Need 20 Prototypes and Later Thousands in Production. Can SigGear Review This?”
docs.text:
Yes. For an applicable custom gearbox or precision transmission project, SigGear can review the prototype requirement together with the expected production path from the beginning.

The first review should include the prototype quantity, expected annual volume, motor / mechanism, target output, installation envelope and schedule if known. Prototype success does not automatically guarantee production readiness; the configuration still needs validation, design freeze, inspection definition and pilot preparation before repeat manufacturing.

docs.title: A Custom Transmission Project Is Not Finished When the First Sample Moves
docs.text:
For an engineering team, the first prototype answers only one question:

Can this transmission concept work well enough to continue evaluating?

A production-ready configuration requires more than a successful first sample. The motor, gearbox, ratio, mechanical interface, operating point, materials, driver / encoder configuration where applicable, drawings and inspection requirements need to converge into a controlled configuration that can be manufactured repeatedly.

SigGear works with engineers through this development path for applicable compact transmission projects. The objective is not only to produce a functional sample, but to develop a controlled configuration that can move into repeatable manufacturing when the project reaches production. Projects that begin with tens of prototypes and may later move to hundreds or thousands of units should be reviewed as production programs from the beginning.

Discuss Your Project Send Your Drawing or Requirement

docs.title: Start From the Transmission Architecture
docs.text:
If the transmission architecture is already known, continue with the relevant engineering path:

docs.title: Typical Development Path
docs.text:
A project may move through:

Idea / Requirement / Existing Design → Feasibility Review → Transmission Architecture Review → Preliminary Configuration → Prototype / Sample → Application Test → Design Iteration → Design Freeze / Design-In → Pilot Preparation → Production Release

The exact sequence depends on how mature the customer's design already is.

A project based on an existing SigGear platform may move faster than a project that requires a different motor, ratio, interface or transmission architecture.

Starting from customer geometry? Custom Gearbox From Drawing / STEP / Sample explains what SigGear can review from a 2D drawing, STEP model or physical sample before prototype development.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Idea, Drawing or Existing Mechanism
docs.text:
The first discussion can start from:

  • a product idea
  • an existing mechanism
  • a customer motor
  • a current gearbox that needs to be replaced
  • a STEP model or drawing
  • a space envelope
  • a torque / speed target
  • a prototype that does not yet meet the required performance

A complete transmission specification is not required before the first engineering discussion.

Useful starting information includes:

  • application
  • what needs to move
  • load or torque requirement if known
  • output speed
  • available diameter and length
  • operating voltage where applicable
  • existing motor or controller if already selected
  • shaft and mounting constraints
  • prototype quantity
  • expected production volume if known

docs.title: Stage 2 — Feasibility Review
docs.text:
The purpose of feasibility review is to determine whether the project has a credible engineering path before committing to a final configuration.

The review may include:

  • planetary vs. cycloidal transmission structure
  • existing SigGear platform vs. modified configuration
  • motor suitability
  • preliminary ratio
  • size and packaging
  • output interface
  • bearing and external-load conditions
  • driver / encoder architecture where applicable
  • parameters that still need calculation or testing

The result of this stage is not a guaranteed final design. It is a decision about which concept deserves further engineering work.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Preliminary Configuration
docs.text:
Once the architecture is selected, the project can be narrowed into a prototype configuration.

Depending on the product family, this may define:

  • gearbox frame size
  • stage count and ratio
  • motor
  • motor-to-gearbox interface
  • output shaft or flange
  • mounting pattern
  • housing or packaging arrangement
  • encoder / sensor configuration
  • driver configuration
  • cable and connector arrangement
  • communication interface where applicable

At this stage, some details may still be provisional.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Prototype or Sample
docs.text:
The first prototype should be built around a clear engineering question.

Examples:

  • does the assembly fit the available space?
  • does the motor + gearbox combination reach the required output speed?
  • does the joint handle the representative load?
  • does the selected ratio provide the expected motion?
  • does the shaft or flange interface work with the customer's mechanism?
  • does the selected driver / encoder configuration integrate with the controller?

The sample should not be treated as a frozen production design simply because it can rotate or transmit load.

Open the Sample Validation Workflow

docs.title: Stage 5 — Application Test
docs.text:
The prototype should be evaluated in the actual or representative mechanism.

Useful test conditions may include:

  • continuous load
  • peak load and peak duration
  • output speed
  • acceleration and deceleration
  • duty cycle
  • direction reversals
  • radial / axial loads
  • temperature
  • current where applicable
  • noise or vibration where relevant
  • backlash or positioning behavior where relevant
  • encoder / communication behavior
  • power-off behavior if important

A test result is meaningful only when the operating condition is recorded.

docs.title: Stage 6 — Design Iteration
docs.text:
A prototype that reveals a problem is not automatically a failed project.

The purpose of engineering validation is to identify what must change before the next build.

Depending on the project, iteration may involve:

  • ratio
  • motor
  • output shaft
  • mounting pattern
  • housing
  • axial length
  • bearing arrangement
  • cable / connector
  • driver
  • encoder
  • current limit
  • control configuration
  • thermal condition
  • assembly method

A change to one parameter can affect several others. For example, changing motor speed or ratio can affect torque, efficiency, gearbox length, thermal behavior and control settings.

Therefore, revisions should be treated as controlled configuration changes rather than isolated adjustments.

docs.title: Stage 7 — Design Freeze and Design-In
docs.text:
A website status of Design-In Review Ready means the project is ready to be submitted for formal engineering review. It is not the same as Design Frozen. Design Freeze must be confirmed by the responsible project / engineering teams against the exact controlled configuration and revision.

Before the transmission is treated as designed into the customer's product, the exact configuration should be identifiable.

Typical items to freeze include:

  • product / project configuration
  • reduction ratio
  • motor
  • output interface
  • motor-side interface
  • envelope dimensions
  • mounting features
  • driver and encoder where applicable
  • cable and connector configuration
  • firmware / protocol revision where applicable
  • approved operating conditions
  • drawing revision

The goal is to make sure the customer, SigGear engineering and manufacturing teams are all referring to the same configuration.

Open the Design-In Checklist

docs.title: Stage 8 — Pilot Preparation
docs.text:
Pilot Preparation Ready is a manually confirmed project milestone. It should only follow a confirmed Design Freeze plus agreement on pilot quantity, schedule, inspection requirements, change control and any project-specific documentation.

Before a pilot build, the project should move from an engineering sample mindset toward repeatable manufacturing.

Items that may need confirmation include:

  • controlled drawing revision
  • configuration / BOM definition
  • inspection characteristics
  • incoming or outgoing test requirements
  • critical dimensions
  • assembly requirements
  • cable / connector definition
  • labeling or packaging requirements where relevant
  • pilot quantity
  • delivery schedule
  • change-control expectations

The exact documentation scope depends on the project and must be agreed with the customer.

Open Pilot Preparation Review

docs.title: Stage 9 — Production Release
docs.text:
A custom transmission should enter regular production only after the configuration and commercial scope have been confirmed.

Production release may require confirmation of:

  • final approved configuration
  • technical agreement or controlled drawing
  • order quantity
  • forecast or expected demand where available
  • manufacturing and inspection requirements
  • packaging / labeling requirements where applicable
  • approved changes from the prototype or pilot stage

SigGear does not treat an early sample, preliminary drawing or feasibility concept as an automatic production approval.

Open Production Release Review

Production Released remains a human-confirmed project / manufacturing milestone. A complete website checklist can only mean the release package is ready to be submitted for review.

docs.title: What Engineers Can Change During Development
docs.text:
Depending on the platform and engineering feasibility, development may include review of:

Area Examples Transmission planetary / cycloidal structure, ratio, stage count Motor motor type, speed, power and mechanical interface Packaging diameter, length, housing and installation envelope Input shaft, pinion, pilot and mounting interface Output shaft, flange, mounting pattern and locating features Bearing / load radial, axial and overturning load arrangement Feedback Hall / encoder configuration where supported Driver / control integrated or external driver and supported control functions Connection cable, connector and communication interface Operating target torque, speed, backlash, duty cycle and thermal condition

Not every parameter can be changed independently, and not every requested change is feasible on every product platform.

docs.title: The Goal Is Repeatable Production, Not Only a Working Sample
docs.text:
For customer programs that progress beyond prototype validation, the engineering work must connect to manufacturing:

  • controlled configuration and drawing revision
  • repeatable component manufacturing
  • assembly process definition
  • inspection requirements
  • pilot build preparation
  • production scheduling
  • batch delivery planning

Production capacity and lead time are project-specific, but SigGear's manufacturing role is intended to support the transition from custom engineering into repeat production rather than stopping at a one-off prototype.

Custom Manufacturing & Volume Production

docs.title: Existing Platforms Can Shorten the Development Path
docs.text:
A project does not always require a completely new transmission.

Existing SigGear products can be used as engineering starting points.

Examples include:

  • 8-42 mm planetary gearbox platforms for miniature and compact gear drives
  • 32P with public motor-integration and mechanical-interface resources
  • SG-6010C / SG-6010D / SG-8021 planetary robot-joint reference platforms
  • CPM-80-25 / CPM-100-25 / CPM-78-39 cycloidal reference platforms

A project may use one of these products directly, modify the surrounding interface, or use the platform as a reference while another configuration is evaluated.

Open Custom Precision Transmission Engineering Open the Engineering Center

docs.title: Confidentiality and Customer Designs
docs.text:
Custom development often involves unreleased products, customer CAD, proprietary mechanisms and future production plans.

These projects may be protected by confidentiality agreements and therefore cannot be shown publicly.

SigGear uses public reference products, engineering resources, manufacturing information and released test data to show its technical capabilities without exposing confidential customer designs.

docs.title: What SigGear Does Not Assume
docs.text:
Before a project reaches production release, do not assume that:

  • the first prototype is the final production configuration
  • a measured short-duration test point is a continuous rating
  • a driver feature from one model applies to another
  • a public simplified STEP replaces a controlled production drawing
  • a requested customization is feasible without engineering review
  • a prototype quantity automatically defines production MOQ or pricing
  • an application area listed on the website represents a public customer case

docs.text:
